children: By Staff Writer

Tourism stakeholders in East Africa are calling for urgent reforms to reduce the cost of travel across the region, saying high airfares, expensive cross-border transactions and slow implementation of regional agreements are undermining efforts to build a single tourism market.

Industry players want East African Community (EAC) governments to improve air connectivity, enable seamless digital payments and remove policy barriers that continue to limit movement between member states.
They are also calling for the implementation of Article 104 of the EAC Treaty, which provides for cooperation on the free movement of people, labour, services and goods.

The proposals emerged from discussions involving tourism operators, policymakers and private-sector players from Kenya and Uganda in Mombasa this week. The issues are expected to be presented at a regional tourism summit scheduled for October 26-27, bringing together governments and industry representatives to seek practical solutions.
Herbert Kiguli, Uganda's Consul in Mombasa, said the increase in movement between Kenya and Uganda demonstrated the potential of regional tourism if the remaining barriers were removed.
He said the use of national identification cards for cross-border travel had helped increase movement between the two countries.
Uganda has remained one of Kenya's biggest regional source markets, with more than 225,000 visitors recorded in 2024 and 234,556 in 2025.
The visitors include business and conference travellers, people visiting friends and relatives, and leisure tourists heading to the Kenyan coast.

Mr Kiguli said the numbers could grow further if governments implemented policies agreed under the EAC integration framework."We need to look at the policies that have been on the shelf and see how they can help us increase tourism numbers," he said.
He said technology should be used to remove some of the financial and administrative barriers facing travellers, particularly in payments.

A tourist crossing from Uganda into Kenya should be able to use a mobile phone to pay for accommodation, transport, restaurants and other services without facing high currency conversion or transaction charges, he said.

Stakeholders want mobile money platforms such as Safaricom's M-Pesa paybill and MTN MoMo Pay to become interoperable across borders. As it is, one can send money to numbers across the region but payments to tills is not yet interoperable between countries."We need to use mobile technology to support a cashless economy," he said.
The push comes as tourism becomes increasingly dependent on digital platforms for bookings, payments and marketing.

Stakeholders want young people to play a bigger role in promoting East Africa online, using social media, online travel platforms and mobile applications to market attractions across national borders.
They argue that Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania and other EAC countries should be promoted as complementary destinations rather than competing individually for visitors.
The EAC Secretariat has also been urged to use technology to address policy bottlenecks and improve the visitor experience, from booking and payment to border crossing, transport and accommodation.
However, air transport remains a major obstacle.
Kenya Association of Tour Operators (KATO) Coast representative Patrick Kamanga said that high airfares were making travel within East Africa unnecessarily expensive.

He cited the Mombasa-Entebbe route, where fares can reach $800."Mombasa to Entebbe fares do not make sense at all. You can pay almost $800, which is equivalent to travelling to Europe," Mr Kamanga said.

He called on EAC countries to treat their airspace as a single market and eliminate national taxes and charges that raise the cost of regional flights."We need to enter the region as one bloc and eliminate these taxes at the national level," he said.
Mr Kamanga said airline operating rights within the region should also be reviewed, while governments improve roads, airports and other infrastructure connecting tourist destinations.
Access, he said, remained a major challenge, noting that a visitor may enter one country easily but face expensive or unreliable transport when trying to reach another destination within the region.
The October summit is expected to bring together national and county governments, airlines, tour operators, hoteliers and other private-sector players to identify bottlenecks.
